chief_complaint: seeking detox, severe body aches, runny nose, pupil dilation
hpi_details: A 77-year-old male presents to the clinic with seeking detox, severe body aches, runny nose, pupil dilation. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: He thinks his severe body aches and sweats are withdrawal symptoms because he abruptly ran out of his prescription pain pills.
concerns: He is worried that his family will find out he has become dependent on painkillers and lose respect for him.
expectations: He hopes the doctor can prescribe medication to stop the agonizing body aches and help him safely detox without having to go into a hospital facility.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Opioid Use Disorder evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Opioid Use Disorder is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes COWS scoring and initiation of buprenorphine-naloxone only when objective moderate withdrawal is present, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: seeking detox, severe body aches, runny nose, pupil dilation

Key HPI features: A 77-year-old male presents to the clinic with seeking detox, severe body aches, runny nose, pupil dilation. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Opioid Use Disorder.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Opioid Use Disorder.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Adjustment disorder without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Acute suicidal or homicidal ideation.
management_principles: Use COWS scoring; initiate buprenorphine-naloxone when moderate objective withdrawal is present to avoid precipitated withdrawal
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with chief complaint of seeking detox, severe body aches, runny nose, pupil dilation. HPI: opioid use disorder.
reference_soap.objective: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Opioid Use Disorder.
reference_soap.assessment: Condition highly suspicious for Opioid Use Disorder.
reference_soap.plan: A qualified clinician should assess withdrawal severity, recent opioid exposure, co-ingestants, medical stability, and overdose risk before initiating medication for opioid use disorder. Provide overdose education and naloxone, and arrange ongoing addiction treatment; urgently evaluate reduced consciousness, slow breathing, chest pain, or suicidality.

Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Opioid Use Disorder

must_ask.say: What have you been using, and when was your last dose?
Are you having body aches, a runny nose, or chills right now?
How long have you been using, and how do you typically take it?
Have you tried methadone or buprenorphine treatment before?
Do you have any other medical conditions or medications we should know about during your detox, given your age?

history.answer: I need help getting off pain medications, doctor. My whole body aches, my nose keeps running, and I feel completely miserable.
I take oxycodone tablets that I swallow. I do not inject, crush, or snort them.
I have been taking about 60 to 80 milligrams every single day, spread out into three or four doses.
It started two years ago after spinal surgery; over time, the original dose stopped working, so I had to keep taking more to feel any relief.
I took my last oxycodone pill yesterday afternoon, about twenty hours ago.
I tried stopping completely on my own last week, but the sickness and intense cravings forced me to start taking them again.
Whenever the medication wears off, I get an intense urge to take another pill, and I end up taking much more than I ever intended.
I only drink an occasional beer at family dinners, never felt guilty about drinking, and never needed a drink in the morning.
I have been spending too much of my retirement savings buying pills, and my daughter is upset with me, though I have never driven under the influence.
I have terrible muscle and bone aches, cold sweats with goosebumps, a runny nose, watery eyes, and an upset stomach with loose stools.
No, I have never had a seizure, and I have never seen or heard things that were not actually there.
No, I have never lost consciousness, stopped breathing, or required emergency treatment for an overdose.
I have never used needles or injected any drugs, and I have not had any risky sexual exposures.
No, I have never turned yellow, never vomited blood or passed black stool, and my memory has been fine.
No, I do not take sleeping pills, sedatives, stimulants, or any other recreational drugs.
I feel anxious and embarrassed about this addiction, but I am not clinically depressed and have never thought about ending my life.
This is my very first time seeking medical help or detoxification; I have never been to rehab or a support group.
I want to be free of these pills for my health and to be there for my grandchildren; I am fully determined to quit with medical supervision.
I live alone, but my daughter lives nearby, visits weekly, and is very supportive of me getting clean.
I do not have any chronic heart, lung, liver, or kidney problems that I know of.
Aside from chronic lower back discomfort, my medical history has been completely unremarkable.
I had lumbar spine surgery about two years ago, which is when I was first prescribed painkillers, but no other surgeries.
I do not take any regular prescription medications or over-the-counter supplements right now, only the oxycodone pills.
I have no known allergies to any medications or foods.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used tobacco products in my life.
I only have a small glass of wine or beer once or twice a month during family holidays.
I am retired from clerical work and live independently in an apartment.
There is no family history of substance abuse, mental health disorders, or chronic illnesses.
I think my body is crashing and going through terrible withdrawal because I ran out of the strong pain pills I've been taking.
I'm terrified that my children will find out I got hooked on these pills and look at me with shame.
I'm hoping you can give me something safe to stop these horrible aches and shakes so I can get clean quietly.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 136/84 mmHg, heart rate 92 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, temperature 37.0 C.
Elderly man appearing uncomfortable and restless, with mild diaphoresis, repeated yawning, and clear nasal discharge.
Pupils are bilaterally dilated to approximately 5 mm, equal and reactive to light, with prominent lacrimation and no nystagmus.
Sclerae are anicteric and conjunctivae are clear with excessive tearing.
Moist skin with visible piloerection on both forearms; no needle track marks, cutaneous abscesses, or spider angiomas.
Mild bilateral fine postural tremor visible in outstretched hands, with no asterixis.
Sinus tachycardia with regular rhythm, normal S1 and S2, and no audible murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Abdomen is soft, non-distended, and non-tender, with hyperactive bowel sounds and no palpable hepatosplenomegaly.
Alert, fully oriented to person, place, and time, exhibiting anxious affect without cognitive impairment or perceptual disturbances.
Gait is steady and coordinated without ataxia, and Romberg test is negative.
